s: Cover a kitchen floor with square tiles that are 1 foot on each side. The number of tiles is the *area*. Each tile is a *unit square*. A rectangle that is 4 squares tall and 6 squares wide has 6, 12, 18 and 24 squares, so its area is 24 *square units*. The squares must cover the shape with no gaps and no overlaps. Count every square inside, not just the border.
m: Area is not only for floors. A farmer talks about the area of a field. A painter figures out the area of a wall to know how much paint to buy. In every case the question is the same: how many unit squares would it take to cover the surface? A shape does not need straight sides to have an area. A leaf has an area too, even though counting its squares is harder because the edge cuts some of them.

s: Counting squares one by one is slow, so look at the rows. A bed 7 feet wide and 8 feet long has 7 rows with 8 squares in each. That is 7 × 8 = 56 square feet. Call one side the *length* and the other the *width*. The *formula* is Area = length × width. A rectangle 9 cm by 6 cm has an area of 9 × 6 = 54 square centimeters. Multiply the sides. Do not add them.
m: Why does multiplying work? Every row has the same number of squares, so adding the rows is the same as multiplying. This is why rectangles are so handy. Two measurements are enough to know the whole area, and you never need to count each tile. Try it on a sticky note. Measure its two sides in centimeters with a ruler and multiply. The answer tells you how many centimeter squares would cover it.

s: Match the unit to the size of the thing. Measure small things, like a stamp, in *square centimeters* or square inches. Measure rooms in square feet or *square meters*. Measure cities in *square miles*. A bigger unit holds many smaller ones. A square foot is 12 inches by 12 inches, so it holds 12 × 12 = 144 square inches. A square yard holds 3 × 3 = 9 square feet. The numbers multiply by themselves, not just by 12 or 3. A rug that is 2 by 3 yards has 6 square yards, which is 6 × 9 square feet.
m: Metric units follow the same pattern. A meter is 100 centimeters, so a square meter holds 100 × 100 = 10,000 square centimeters. When each side gets 100 times longer, the area gets 100 × 100 times larger. This is why a square mile is so huge. It is a square with a whole mile on each side, and 1 mile is 5,280 feet.

s: Walk a string around the class garden: 8 feet, 5 feet, 8 feet and 5 feet. The walk is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 feet. That distance around is the *perimeter*. Add every side and skip none. A triangle with sides of 5, 7 and 9 cm has a perimeter of 21 cm. A rectangle has two pairs of equal sides, and a square has four equal sides. Perimeter is a length, so it uses plain units like feet, not square units.
m: Perimeter shows up all around us. A frame needs wood along every edge. A ribbon around a gift needs as much length as the edges it wraps. A fence has to go all the way around a yard. To check your answer, mark one corner and trace around the shape with your finger, adding each side as you pass it. You should end back at your starting corner with every side counted once.

s: A rectangle has two lengths and two widths. Instead of adding four numbers, add the length and width once, then *double* it. For a 12 by 5 rectangle, 12 + 5 = 17, and 17 doubled is 34. The formula is Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). Do the parentheses first. For a cost, find the perimeter, then multiply by the price per foot. Going backward, half the perimeter is length plus width.
m: Why does the shortcut work? Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so going around it means walking one length and one width, and then doing the same again. Perimeter tells you how much fence, trim or border to buy, because the price depends on how many feet you buy and not on the space inside. Try it on a rectangle in your notebook. Measure with a ruler, use the shortcut, then add all four sides to see whether both ways agree.

s: Say the class has exactly 12 seed packets, one for each square foot. A 1 by 12 bed, a 2 by 6 bed and a 3 by 4 bed all have an area of 12 square feet. Their perimeters are different: 26, 16 and 14 feet. Same area, different fence. It works the other way too. A 1 by 7 rectangle and a 4 by 4 *square* both have a perimeter of 16, but their areas are 7 and 16. The shape closest to a square gives the most area for the least fence.
m: Why does a nearly square shape need the least fence? A long, skinny bed has a lot of edge for the space inside, so almost every square foot touches the fence. A bed closer to a square keeps more of its squares in the middle, away from the edge. That is why a builder checks both the area and the perimeter before buying materials.

s: An L-shape has no single formula, but it is two rectangles stuck together. Cut it into pieces you know, find each area and add. This is finding the area of a *composite* shape. A 10 by 4 rectangle and a 6 by 3 rectangle give 40 + 18 = 58 square feet. Sometimes it is easier to subtract. A 6 by 6 square with a 2 by 3 notch cut out has an area of 36 − 6 = 30. The key idea is to *decompose* the hard shape into easy pieces. Label each piece so none is forgotten.
m: Builders do something like this with the plans of a house. A house is rarely one big rectangle, so they can split it into rooms and hallways, find each area and add them up. The place you cut does not change the total. Two students can split the same L in two different ways and still get the same area. If your answers differ, one of you probably forgot a piece or counted one twice.

s: Sometimes a side is missing, so work backward from what you know. A bed has an area of 45 square feet and one side of 5 feet. Since Area = length × width, ask what 5 times what makes 45. It is 45 ÷ 5 = 9 feet. With perimeter, half the perimeter is length plus width. If the perimeter is 30 and the length is 10, then 15 − 10 = 5 feet is the width. A square with an area of 64 has a side that times itself makes 64. That side is 8.
m: Working backward is how you solve many puzzles in daily life. If you know a movie is 90 minutes long and it ended at 4:00, you can go back to find when it began. Math does the same thing with steps that undo each other. Division undoes multiplication, and subtraction undoes addition. After you find a missing side, put it back into the formula to see whether the answer matches what you were told.

s: Soil fills a raised bed in three directions: length, width and height. Flat tiles cannot measure that, so we use *unit cubes*, which are 1 unit long, wide and tall. The number of cubes that pack a box is its *volume*. A box with a floor of 4 by 3 cubes has 12 cubes in one *layer*. If it is 2 cubes tall, it has 2 layers, so 12 + 12 = 24 cubes. The volume is 24 *cubic units*. The word cubic tells you it is volume. Count one full layer, then multiply by the number of layers.
m: Volume matters whenever something has to fit inside. A moving truck, a fish tank and a lunch box all have volume, and it tells how much each one can hold. Cubes make a good unit because they stack with no gaps. A ball would leave gaps between the pieces, and those gaps would make the counting messy. A cubic centimeter is a tiny cube that is 1 centimeter on every edge.

s: Counting layers leads to a shortcut. The floor of a box is a rectangle with an area of length × width, and each layer holds that many cubes. Multiply by the height to count every layer. A box is a *rectangular prism*, and Volume = length × width × height. A planter 8 by 2 by 1 feet holds 8 × 2 × 1 = 16 cubic feet. You can multiply in any order. The floor's area times the height is *base area* times height. Do not add the three numbers, and write cubic in the label.
m: A cube is a special box whose length, width and height are all the same. A cube with edges of 3 units has a volume of 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic units. Notice that 27 is much bigger than the 3 you started with. Volume grows fast. If you double every edge of a box, the volume does not double. Eight times as many cubes fit inside.

s: Pepper's cage is 4 feet long, but the store lists cages in inches. To *convert* feet to inches, multiply, because 1 foot is 12 inches. So 4 × 12 = 48 inches. A *yard* is 3 feet, or 36 inches. A *mile* is 5,280 feet. To go from small units to big ones, divide. An 84-inch rope is 84 ÷ 12 = 7 feet. Ask yourself: should I get more units or fewer?
m: Why does a bigger unit give a smaller number? Because each big unit holds many small ones. Think of a dollar and pennies. One dollar is worth the same as 100 pennies, but you need 100 of the small coins. If you measure a table in inches, you get a bigger number than if you measure it in feet, even though the table did not change. Only the size of the unit changed.

s: The guinea pig food bag says 2 *kilograms*, and the chart says 40 *grams* a day. To compare them, convert. A kilogram is 1,000 grams, so 2 kilograms is 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 grams. Kilo means one thousand, so a *kilometer* is 1,000 meters. A *meter* is 100 centimeters. Mixed amounts convert piece by piece: 2 kilograms 300 grams is 2,000 + 300 = 2,300 grams. Going backward, 5,000 meters is 5,000 ÷ 1,000 = 5 kilometers.
m: Metric prefixes follow a pattern, and learning it helps with many words. Kilo means one thousand times as much. Centi means one hundredth, and milli means one thousandth. So a centimeter is one hundredth of a meter, and a millimeter is one thousandth of a meter. When you meet a metric word you do not know, look at its prefix first. It tells you how big or small the unit is compared with the plain meter or gram.

s: Pepper's water bottle holds 250 *milliliters*. A *liter* is 1,000 milliliters, so a 2-liter bottle holds 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 milliliters. In U.S. kitchens, a *pint* is 2 cups. The bigger units are *quarts and gallons*. A quart is 2 pints, which is 4 cups, and a gallon is 4 quarts, which is 16 cups. To convert, follow the chain one step at a time. Three gallons is 12 quarts, which is 24 pints.
m: A liter and a quart are close in size, but they are not the same. A liter is a little more than a quart. That is why a store shelf can hold a 1-liter bottle next to a 1-quart carton, and the two look almost alike. The metric system makes changing units easier, because every step is a power of ten. Going from liters to milliliters is only multiplying by 1,000, while going from gallons to cups takes several different steps.

s: An *hour* is 60 *minutes*, a day is 24 hours and a week is 7 days. To change hours to minutes, multiply by 60. Pepper's 3 hours of play is 3 × 60 = 180 minutes. To change minutes to hours, divide by 60 and keep the remainder. A 150-minute movie is 2 hours with 30 minutes left over, so it is 2 hours 30 minutes. Two days is 2 × 24 = 48 hours. Time is not like money: 1 hour 30 minutes is 1 and a half hours.
m: Why is time counted in 60s and 24s instead of tens? The 60 comes from the ancient Babylonians, who counted in sixties, and we still use that idea for minutes and hours. The numbers 60 and 24 split evenly in many ways, which is handy. An hour can be cut into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths, and each piece is a whole number of minutes.

s: *Elapsed time* is the time that passes between a start and an end. Do not subtract clock times like ordinary numbers, because 60 minutes make an hour, not 100. Jump along a *number line* of time instead. Math class runs from 9:45 to 11:20. Jump 15 minutes to 10:00, then 1 hour to 11:00, then 20 minutes to 11:20. That adds up to 1 hour 35 minutes. Always jump to a round time first, forward or backward. From 10:50, jump 10 minutes to 11:00 and 25 more to 11:25.
m: Jumping to a round time works because round times are easy to count from. Landing on an hour or a half hour turns a hard subtraction into small, friendly steps. Many people do this in their heads every day, such as when they figure out how long until a bus comes or how long they have been waiting. Try drawing your own time line with arrows, one for each jump, and write the minutes above every arrow.

s: Room 12 voted on a name for a second guinea pig and showed the votes on a *bar graph*. The taller the bar, the more votes. Read the *scale* first. The scale went 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, so each line stood for 5 votes, not 1. Biscuit's bar reached the third line, so it got 3 × 5 = 15 votes. Nugget's reached the second line, so 10 votes. Biscuit beat Nugget by 15 − 10 = 5 votes. Never just count lines.
m: A bar graph is a good picture for comparing groups, because your eye can see which bar is tallest in an instant. The bars stand on a line and all have the same width, so only the height carries the message. This is why the scale matters so much. If the scale started at a number other than 0, the bars could make a small difference look very large. Check where the scale begins.

s: A *picture graph* uses small pictures instead of bars. The *key* tells how many each picture stands for. In the class's March book graph, each book picture stands for 4 books. Maya's row shows 3 pictures, so 3 × 4 = 12 books. A half picture stands for half of 4, which is 2. Leo's row shows 2 whole books and a half, so 2 × 4 + 2 = 10 books. Do not count each picture as 1. Always read the key first.
m: Picture graphs are friendly because a row of pictures lets you see a count. But when numbers are big, the key matters even more. If each picture stood for 1 and there were 200 books, the row would run off the page. A larger key keeps the graph short enough to read. When you make your own picture graph, pick a key that fits your numbers. A key of 2 works well when the counts are all even numbers.

s: Pepper's weight chart is a *line plot*. It has a number line marked in quarters, and each Monday's weight gets an X above its number. A weight that happens again stacks a new X on top. Add all the X marks to count the measurements. The tallest stack is the most common value, not the biggest one. The biggest is the X farthest right. The *range* is the largest value minus the smallest. Pepper's weights went from 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 pounds, so the range is 1 pound.
m: A line plot uses fractions because many real measurements fall between whole numbers. A pencil is not exactly 5 inches long, and a guinea pig is not exactly 2 pounds. Measuring to the nearest half or quarter lets you record what you see without pretending to be exact. The marks on the number line are equal steps apart, so you can count them like the marks on a ruler. When the X marks bunch together in one place, the measurements are close in size.

s: To make a line plot, first measure. The class measured 8 pencils to the nearest half inch: 5, 4 1/2, 6, 5, 5 1/2, 4 1/2, 5 and 6. Find the smallest and largest, 4 1/2 and 6. Draw a number line with every half inch from 4 1/2 to 6. Go through the list and place one X for each pencil, stacking repeats. Check that your X marks add up to 8. Give the plot a *title* and a *label* for the unit. Keep every mark, even an empty one, or the spacing will lie.
m: Once the plot is made, you can read stories in it. Where are the X marks piled up? Are there any lonely X marks far from the rest? A pencil that is much longer or shorter than the others might be a new pencil, or one that has been sharpened many times. Data does not tell you why, but it points you toward good questions to ask.

s: A graph gives you numbers, but you choose the math. Pepper's line plot shows 9 weights. To find the Mondays she weighed less than 2 pounds, add the X marks left of 2: 1 + 2 = 3. Some questions take two steps. Votes were Biscuit 15, Nugget 10, Oreo 8 and Waffles 4. For the votes not for Biscuit, add the others, 10 + 8 + 4 = 22, or take the total of 37 and subtract 15. Both routes agree. Then check *reasonableness*. No answer about 8 pencils can be bigger than 8.
m: Estimating first is a good habit. Before you add 12 + 9 + 6, you might think, that is a little more than 25. If your answer comes out as 270, you know right away that a digit slipped. An estimate does not have to be exact. It only has to be close enough to catch a big mistake. A quick estimate can also help when you are not sure which operation to use.
